title: Check yourself: the Java Memory Model

questions.stem: A feed handler caches a parsed header in a plain field: `if (header == null) header = parse(raw); return header;`, where `parse` never returns null. A load test calls this from 32 threads, five billion times in all, on x86 servers running HotSpot, and it never returns null. What does that run establish?

options.text: That it can't return null on any JVM, since five billion racing calls would have produced every outcome the memory model allows
options.says: a run shows what one JIT did on one CPU; the JMM allows outcomes that five billion calls never showed

options.text: That it can't return null on any x86 JVM, since the memory model leaves outcomes to the CPU, and x86 keeps two reads of one address in order
options.says: the JMM is defined over reads and the writes they may see, not over a CPU; a compiler may reorder the two reads even where the hardware wouldn't

options.text: Only that this JVM on these CPUs didn't return null, since the memory model lets the second read see an older write than the first read saw
options.says: nothing orders two plain reads of one field against another thread's write, so the second read may return the default null after the first saw the header

options.text: Only that this JVM on these CPUs didn't return null, since the memory model lets a reference be read half from one write and half from another
options.says: reads and writes of references are always atomic; the risk is the second read returning an older write

origin.section: The JMM Says Which Writes a Read May Return, and a Test Shows Only Some of Them

questions.stem: A booking service keeps the number of free seats in a volatile int field, and every method reads and writes that field directly: `if (seatsLeft > 0) { seatsLeft = seatsLeft - 1; confirm(); }`. No other field is shared. One seat is left when two customers book at the same moment. What can happen?

options.text: Both bookings are confirmed, since a program without data races still runs as an interleaving, and both checks can come before either write
options.says: every access is volatile, so the program is race-free and sequentially consistent; one of its interleavings has both threads read 1 before either writes

options.text: Both bookings are confirmed, since a volatile read can still return a value that another thread's volatile write has already replaced
options.says: a volatile read sees the latest volatile write before it; the problem is the interleaving of check and write, not a stale read

options.text: Only one booking is confirmed, since a program without data races behaves as if each method call ran alone, start to finish
options.says: sequential consistency interleaves single actions, not whole methods; a check and the write that depends on it are two steps

options.text: Only one booking is confirmed, since a volatile read followed by a volatile write of the same field is carried out as one atomic step
options.says: each volatile read and each volatile write is atomic on its own; nothing joins a read and a later write into one step

origin.section: A Program Without Data Races Runs as Some Interleaving of Its Threads

questions.stem: A library's `Session` keeps `long expiresAt` in a plain field; one thread renews it, request threads check it. The library's README says: "Safe without volatile: every JVM we support is 64-bit." Taking the JLS alone as the contract, what is that claim worth?

options.text: The JLS backs it, since a JVM running on 64-bit hardware is required to read and write a long field in a single access
options.says: the JLS lets any JVM treat a plain long write as two 32-bit writes; 64-bit HotSpot not splitting it is an observation, not a promise

options.text: The JLS backs it, since a write can be split only when two threads write the field, and here a single thread renews it
options.says: a reader can combine the halves of two successive writes by the same thread

options.text: The JLS doesn't back it, since it lets any JVM carry out a plain long write as two separate writes of 32 bits each
options.says: JLS 17.7 treats a write to a non-volatile long or double as two writes, one per 32-bit half, whatever the hardware

options.text: The JLS doesn't back it, since it lets any JVM carry out a write wider than a byte as several separate writes
options.says: only plain long and double may be split; int, reference and smaller writes are atomic, and neighbouring fields never tear into each other

origin.section: A Plain long or double May Be Read Half Old, Half New

questions.stem: An immutable `Route` lazily caches derived values, each in a plain field that its getter checks for the default value, computes, and stores. Each getter reads its field once into a local and returns the local. Which of these caches can stay a plain field, threads that race simply computing it again?

options.text: An int count of the stops, since every thread computes the same value and stores it with a single write that can't be split
options.says: the value is derived from immutable state, so every write is the same, and an int write is atomic: the conditions String.hashCode relies on

options.text: A long length in metres, since every thread computes the same value and stores it with a single write that can't be split
options.says: a plain long write may be split into two halves, so a reader can see a value made of two writes

options.text: An ArrayList of stop names, filled and then stored, since a reference write is atomic and the list is complete before it
options.says: ArrayList's fields aren't final, so nothing orders the filling before the plain reference write; a reader may see the reference and not the contents

options.text: An ArrayList of stop names, stored and then filled, since a reference write is atomic and readers see the stops as they are added
options.says: a reader can see the list before it is complete, and the list is mutable shared state with no ordering at all

origin.section: A Race Is Benign Only When Every Thread Writes the Same Value, in One Indivisible Write, Read Once
